SUE Design Manager User Guide

Chapter 2

Wires And Buses

Introduction

Wires are used in SUE to represent connectivity. In this chapter, we will cover how wires and busses are named.

Wires and Buses

Wires in SUE inherit the name of any attached and named I/O or global terminal. (Unnamed I/O or global terminals will flag an error, and will otherwise be ignored.) If neither exists, SUE will generate a unique name of the form net_<number> or uc_net_<number> for netlisting purposes.

Nets are assigned uc_net_<number>, for unconnected net, if they are only connected to one terminal (remember that I/O's are also icons so a wire connected from a terminal to a gate is not unconnected) and SUE will emit a warning in the SUE command window alerting you to any unconnected nets during netlisting. If you have a net that is giving you an unconnected net warning and the net is correct, you have a number of choices:

  • Ignore the warning.

  • Add a name_net icon without a name to the net.

  • You can tell SUE to ignore reporting unconnected nets on certain pins that typically don't get connected by adding the pin names to the list NETLIST(ignore_unconnected) in your .suerc file. For example, you might add scan_in to this list.

  • You can turn off all netlist warnings for unconnected nets by setting NETLIST(warning) to 0 in your .suerc file. Note that you will still see unconnected net warnings from cached files if you do this.

Globals should only be used for constants and power supplies as they are not included in the input/output specifications of the cell when netlisting. SUE recognizes and converts (when needed) Verilog constant syntax of the form: 

              <# of bits>'(b|o|h|d)<number> 
     

as, for example: 

              2'b0 
              4'hdf 
              4'd11



SUE will also pad numbers, when needed, like 31'b0.

I/O's, Globals, and name_nets cannot overlap - their terminals cannot occupy the exact same SUE grid point. The only exception to this is for I/O's and name_nets that have the exact same name.

  • If you want to name a net that is not otherwise named by an I/O or global, attach a name_net icon to the wire at any place and name the name_net as desired.


    The name_net, name_net_s, and name_net_sw icons are all identical in function but look slightly different. The three icons are provided to enhance the look of your schematics.

Net names are SUE's only clue as to the type of wire - or sometimes its connection. For example, two nets will be netlisted as one if they have the same net name as determined by either the name_net icon, an I/O name, or a global name.

  • This connection of nets "feature" can be used (sparingly) to connect nets together where actual wires may be awkward or clutter the drawing.

Buses are just specially-named wires. The wire itself looks no different whether it's a bus or a wire until you netlist the schematic or you run generate term names on it. Then the buses will be displayed as fat wires. Wires with the following type of names are buses: 

      bus_name[msb:lsb]   or 
      [msb:lsb]           or 
      <name1>,<name2>,... 
     

where "msb" and "lsb" must be integers. (If "msb" and "lsb" are the same, then the wire is not a bus. This is mostly legal syntax but redundant and should be avoided.) "msb" may be smaller than "lsb". Buses made from comma-separated wires, buses, or bus_ranges are called concatenated buses and discussed below.

Individual wires in a given bus can then be specified by one of the following formats: 

      bus_name[num]   or 
      [num]           or 
      <name> 
     

If the bus_name is absent, (for example, [3:0] or [1]), then the bus name is inferred from the rest of the net or, if none is specified, then it is uniquely generated with the form net_# or uc_net_#.

No special icons or incantations are required for composing buses or extracting wires or buses from existing buses. Just name the nets unambiguously and SUE should netlist them correctly. Below is a cleverly constructed example which demonstrates how easy it is:

    Figure 2: Busses in SUE 
     

In this case, the two-bit bus named "bar" enters the schematic via the input terminal on the left. The individual bits of bar are peeled off using the name_net icons named [0] and [1]. There is no need to label these name_net icons bar[0] and bar[1] since the name bar is already inferred from the input, and would, in fact, make it harder to rename the net to something else if you ever wanted to, since you would have to rename three things then instead of just one. However, you may do so if you think it schematic makes the schematic more readable.

On wires with multiple named sections, like the above case, SUE determines the bit/bus designation of each wire or terminal by the following algorithm:

      • A segment of a wire or instance terminal is assigned a name based on the largest (widest bus) of the named terminals connected to it.

      • Wires with similar root names (for example, bus names with "[...]" removed) are connected together.

      • Net names on name_nets on buses without bus specifiers are replaced with the largest bus range.

Small movements of name_nets can produce unwanted results. The following example displays a common example with the correct way and the incorrect way of drawing it:

    Figure 3: Bus Naming

In the "correct" circuit, each of the name_nets, `[0]', `[1]', and `[2]', are connected to the entire bus "[2:0]". In contrast, only `[0]' in the "incorrect" circuit is connected to `[2:0]'. The input terminal on inverter `A' will be arbitrarily connected to either `[2]' or `[1]' since both of these have the same bus width and thus neither is preferred. A similar ambiguity arises with inverter `B'.

If a wire has no bus specification (neither a [msb:lsb] or a "," concatenation), then SUE will check if it is an implicit bus. Implicit buses are inferred by either bused terminals such as `sel[2:0]' or bused instances such as those shown in the following circuit:

    Figure 4: Bussed Icons 
     

All of the wires in this example are implicit 3-bit buses ([2:0]) because all of the terminals are three bits wide (one bit wide times the three-bit wide bused instance). The wire named `foo' is also inferred to be foo[2:0] since no bit specifier is given. If foo were renamed `foo[0]', however, then the wire attached to foo would not be a bus. Instead, all of the outputs of the second inverter would be tied together.

Note that implicit buses are always numbered as [bus_width-1:0]. Thus the wires in the following 2 circuits will still have the same bus designations [2:0] as those above:

    Figure 5: Implicit buses 
     

SUE will also infer buses when the terminals are buses and the icons are not buses, as shown in the following example:

    Figure 6: Terminal Buses 
     

Again, all of wires in this example will be inferred to be three-bit buses [2:0]. Mixing and matching of the above two forms also works as expected.

A common case occurs when you only want to use a subset of an output bus from an icon.

Consider the following example:

    Figure 7: Naming Buses 
     

In this case, you want to ignore bit [2] coming out of `foo'. In order for this to work, you need to label the width of both sides of the net as shown above. This seems redundant but is necessary.

SUE gives precedence to output terminals over input terminals when inferring implicit buses. Typically outputs are never tied together while inputs can be, and thus SUE attempts to follow this circuit design rule. For example, in the following common circuit used to buffer up a tree

    Figure 8: Bused and Non-bused Icons 
     

The wire labeled `a' is not a bus but `b' is inferred to be a bus.

While SUE can't handle two-dimensional buses, it does handle some complicated cases. Below are the three allowable cases with bused input pins:

    Figure 9: More Busing Examples 
     

In all cases the input terminal is a bus and the instance is arrayed. In this example, the input terminal "in" is a two-bit bus and the instance is arrayed 4 times, and hence there are really 8 (2 bits x 4 instances) inputs. In the first case, all 8 inputs are tied to the scalar input `foo'. In the second case, in[1] in each instance is tied to foo[1] and in[0] in each instance is tied to foo[0]. In the last case, foo[7] and foo[6] are tied to in[1] and in[0] in instance [3], foo[5] and foo[4] are tied to in[1] and in[0] in instance [2], and so on.

Note that if you inadvertently use a form that is not consistent with one of the three above, SUE will flag it with a warning during netlisting. For example, if the input pin in the last example were labeled foo[8:0] instead of foo[7:0], SUE would produce the following warning: 

      NETLIST WARNING: illegal bused array size - foo[8:0] into in[1:0] with an instance width of 4.
Concatenated Buses

In actual circuits, you typically need to combine and separate various bits of various buses. SUE allows you to do this using the "," concatenation operator on name_nets, but not on I/O's, globals, or instance names. Buses built from concatenations are based on Verilog syntax rules for concatenation (except you don't need the braces {}). Thus wires, bus ranges, or entire buses can be concatenated by simply writing them in msb-to-lsb order, separated by commas (,).

For example: 

      a,b,c 
       
      foo[3],hi[3:0]  
       
      bar[3],bar[3],bar[2] 
      
     

are all legal bus names. Note that the order of the signals is very important. For example: 

      a,b,c 	 	 	 	 	is not equal to 	 	 	 c,b,a
 
      foo[3],hi[3:0]  	 	 	 	is equal to 	 	 	 	foo[3],hi[3],hi[2],hi[1:0]
 
      bar[3],bar[3],bar[2] 			is equal to 	  	 	 	bar[3],bar[3:2]

Concatenated buses are simply made by adding name_nets with comma-separated names. When connecting concatenated buses to other wires/buses, the names must be a subset/superset of each other. This is illustrated in the following diagram:

    Figure 10: Concatenated Buses

When concatenating buses, you always have to specify the bus root except for the following special case.

    Figure 11: More Concatenated Buses 
     

In this case, it is obvious that the bus root is `a' and thus you don't need to specify it when rearranging the bits with `[2],[3],[0],[1]'.

Bus_combine

If you really need to rename a bus/wire, use the bus_combine icon which will introduce an assign statement into your Verilog netlist or a 0 volt voltage source into your SPICE netlist.

The bus_combine icon uses the assign operator when Verilog netlisting which is a unidirectional operator. Furthermore, some tools that read Verilog netlists don't handle the assign operator.

LVS and other operations on SPICE netlists often don't handle 0 volt voltage sources.

Below is an example of the use of the bus_combine. The `0' denotes the lsb end of the bus combine. This example replaces bit 10 in a 32-bit bus called qux with the input baz:

    Figure 12: Bus Combine Example

This bus combine would create the following assign statement (in Verilog netlisting mode): 

      assign out[31:0] = {qux[31:11],baz,qux[9:0]};

Note that the bus_combine icon is a generator so you can change it to merge as many buses together as you want. You can also change the bus_combine icon to have a width of one if you want to simply rename a bus.

While the bus_combine icon makes it possible to tie an output to an input, you should be very careful in using it this way. While simulators can handle this, few other backend tools can. In general, this is not a good way to add feedthroughs to cells.

Debugging Buses

Sometimes SUE gets confused with more complex buses. Sometimes, the user gets confused about what he or she can and cannot do. How to solve this? Easy, let SUE tell you what it thinks a net name is.

  • Draw your schematic and label your nets.

  • Then hit generate term names in the Sim menu.

  • Now select individual nets and SUE will display what it has determined to be the net name in the message window along with the rest of the selection. If the name is not what you desire, change the circuit and repeat.
